Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Unity Health Partners Q2 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are currently in a listen-only mode. After the speakers' presentation, there will be a question-and-answer session. As a reminder, please do not hesitate to reach out to the conference coordinator prior to or following the call should you have any technical difficulties. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Jordan Lee, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Jordan Lee:
Thank you, operator. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss Unity Health Partners' financial results for the Q2 2024. Joining me on the call are Sarah Thompson, Chief Executive Officer; Michael Chen, Chief Financial Officer; Dr. Elena Vasquez, Chief Medical Officer; and Robert Hayes, Chief Operating Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that certain statements made during this call may contain forward-looking statements within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. These statements are based on management's current expectations and are subject to risks, uncertainties, and other factors that could cause actual results to differ materially. Please refer to our SEC filings for a more detailed discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Sarah Thompson.

Sarah Thompson:
Thank you, Jordan, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. I'm pleased to report on our performance for the Q2 2024. We continue to execute on our strategic priorities, focusing on delivering high-quality patient care, expanding our network, and improving operational efficiency.

Today, I will provide an overview of our key achievements during the quarter, focusing on five key aspects: strategic priorities and outlook for the next quarter/year, operating margin YoY and QoQ, same-facility admissions and patient day growth YoY and QoQ, capital expenditures for facility modernization and expansion, and percentage of revenue from Medicare, Medicaid, commercial insurance, and self-pay.

Let me start with our strategic priorities and outlook for the next quarter and year. As we wrap up a strong Q2 where we delivered 10% year-over-year revenue growth to $2.9 billion—driven by a 7% increase in adjusted admissions and a 5% rise in patient days—I'm excited to outline our strategic priorities and forward guidance for Q3 and the full fiscal year 2024. At Unity Health Partners, our 45-hospital footprint across the Southeast and Midwest positions us uniquely to capitalize on the industry's tailwinds, including demographic aging, the shift to value-based care, and robust elective procedure recovery post-COVID.

Let me break this down into our four core strategic pillars, each underpinned by actionable initiatives, realistic targets, and regional insights.

First, accelerating digital transformation and operational efficiency. We're doubling down on tech-enabled care to combat margin pressures from labor costs, which rose 4.2% industry-wide last year per Kaufman Hall data. In Q2, we achieved a 15% reduction in length-of-stay through our AI-powered predictive analytics platform, integrated with Epic MyChart 2024. We've deployed this across 80% of our facilities, partnering with Google Cloud Healthcare for real-time bed management and sepsis detection—yielding a 12% drop in readmissions, ahead of our CMS benchmarks for the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program.

Looking ahead, we'll roll out robotic-assisted surgery suites from Intuitive Surgical's da Vinci Xi systems in 10 additional hospitals by Q4, targeting a 20% uplift in high-acuity surgical volumes, which carry 2.5x higher reimbursement than outpatient services. This initiative, combined with supply chain optimization via our GPO partnership with Vizient, positions us to expand adjusted EBITDA margins from 12.2% in Q2 to 13-14% for FY24—insulated against the 6-8% medical supply inflation we've seen in pharmaceuticals and orthopedics.

Second, portfolio optimization through M&A and de novo growth. The fragmented $1.2 trillion U.S. hospital market offers consolidation opportunities, much like HCA Healthcare's 2023 acquisitions in high-growth MSAs. We've closed the $450 million tuck-in of three acute-care facilities in the booming Atlanta and Nashville markets, adding 350 licensed beds and improving our payer mix to 52% commercial from 48% last year. This drove a 3-point mix shift, boosting average revenue per admission to $15,200.

For the next 12 months, we anticipate 5-7% organic growth from de novo micro-hospitals in underserved suburban corridors of Florida and Texas, where population growth exceeds 2% annually per U.S. Census data. These 8-16 bed facilities, modeled after HCA's freestanding ER success, emphasize outpatient cardiology and orthopedics—segments growing 12% YoY per Definitive Healthcare. Regionally, our Southeast operations (60% of revenue) remain resilient amid Medicaid redeterminations, with only a 1% dip in volumes versus 3-5% nationally, while Midwest expansion mitigates reimbursement headwinds from Illinois' flat Medicare rates.

Third, advancing value-based care and payer innovation. With 35% of our revenue now at risk under MSSP and CJR bundles—up from 25% two years ago—we're outperforming peers like Tenet Healthcare on quality metrics. Q2 ACO savings hit $45 million, a 22% YoY increase, thanks to our population health platform with Optum, which stratifies 2.5 million attributed lives for chronic condition management. We've seen a 18% reduction in total cost of care for diabetic cohorts, aligning with CMS's push toward global budgets.

Over the next quarter, we'll launch narrow-network contracts with Blue Cross Blue Shield affiliates in three states, targeting 2-3% ASP uplift. FY24 outlook: value-based revenue to reach 45% of total, contributing 150 basis points to EBITDA expansion.

Fourth, talent retention and workforce resilience. Addressing the 10-15% nurse vacancy rates plaguing the industry (per AMN Healthcare), we've invested $120 million in Q2 for wage premiums and travel nurse reductions—cutting agency spend by 28% to $250 million annualized. Our "Unity Clinical Academy" has upskilled 4,000 RNs in tele-ICU protocols, boosting retention to 89% from 82%.

Q3 and FY24 Outlook. For Q3, we guide revenue of $3.0-$3.1 billion (9-12% YoY growth), adjusted admissions up 6-8%, and EBITDA of $390-$420 million (13-13.5% margin). Same-facility metrics remain strong: patient days +4-6%, revenue per patient day +3-4%. Full-year FY24: revenue $12.2-$12.6 billion (10-13% growth), EBITDA $1.65-$1.75 billion (13.2-13.7% margin), with capex at $950 million focused on tech and expansion.

Risks include softer elective volumes if consumer confidence wanes amid 5% unemployment, or reimbursement cuts from the impending Medicare Physician Fee Schedule. But with a fortress balance sheet—net leverage at 2.8x, $1.2 billion liquidity—we're well-positioned.

Now, I’ll turn the call over to Michael Chen to provide a more detailed review of our financial results, including the other key aspects.

Michael Chen:
Thank you, Sarah. Good morning, everyone. As Sarah mentioned, we had a solid quarter. Net revenue for the Q2 2024 was $2.9 billion, an increase of 10% compared to the same period last year. This growth was driven by increased patient volume and improved payer mix.

Our operating expenses were $2.49 billion, representing 86% of net revenue. We are continuing to focus on managing our costs effectively while investing in key growth initiatives, particularly in supply chain optimization.

Net income for the quarter was $285 million, or $1.42 per share. We are pleased with our financial performance and remain confident in our ability to achieve our financial goals for the year.

Let me now dive deeper into some of these metrics, starting with our operating margin, which came in at 12.5% for the quarter—up 220 basis points year-over-year from 10.2% in Q2 2023, and up 70 basis points quarter-over-quarter from 11.8% in Q1 2024. This marks our strongest quarterly operating margin in over two years and reflects the tangible results of our disciplined execution across cost management, revenue optimization, and operational leverage in a still-challenging healthcare environment.

Let me break this down systematically, starting with the year-over-year dynamics. Revenue grew 10% YoY to $2.9 billion, driven primarily by a 6.1% increase in admissions and a 2.4% lift in our case mix index, or CMI, to 1.92—benefiting from higher-acuity procedures like robotic-assisted orthopedics and complex cardiovascular interventions, which now represent 28% of our surgical volume, up from 24% last year. We also saw favorable payer mix shifts, with commercial volumes up 4.7% as patients returned post-COVID deferrals, partially offset by Medicare's 2.7% reimbursement reduction under the IPPS final rule.

On the expense side, this is where our margin expansion truly shone. Total operating expenses rose only 6.5% YoY, well below revenue growth, delivering meaningful leverage. Labor costs, which comprise 52% of our cost base, increased just 4.2% despite industry-wide shortages—thanks to our workforce optimization program, including targeted retention bonuses averaging 8% for critical roles like RNs and respiratory therapists, and a 15% reduction in per diem agency spend through our Unity Talent Network, now covering 85% of our 42,000 FTEs across 45 hospitals. Supply expenses, at 22% of costs, were flat YoY after implementing our AI-driven procurement platform in partnership with Vizient, which optimized pricing on high-volume items like ortho implants and pharma, yielding $28 million in savings—equivalent to 100 basis points of margin.

Other operating costs benefited from our Epic EHR go-lives in 12 facilities, reducing denials by 18% to 4.2% of net revenue through improved coding accuracy and prior auth automation. Quarter-over-quarter, the 70 bps expansion from Q1's 11.8% was fueled by seasonal tailwinds: equivalent patient days grew 3.4% QoQ on stronger elective volumes, while bad debt expense dipped to 2.8% of revenue amid stabilizing consumer confidence. We also realized $12 million in quarterly efficiencies from our outpatient shift strategy, with ambulatory surgery centers now handling 32% of procedures—mirroring trends at peers like HCA and driven by our 14 new ASC developments this year.

Regionally, performance varied but trended positively overall. In our Southeast core markets—Florida, Texas, and Georgia, which account for 62% of EBITDA—margins hit 14.8%, up 310 bps YoY, propelled by robust commercial payer mix (45% of revenue) and lower LOS at 4.2 days versus the national average of 4.6. Texas, in particular, benefited from Medicaid redeterminations post-pandemic unwind, adding 150 bps. Conversely, our Northeast urban cluster—New York and Massachusetts, 18% of the portfolio—saw margins at 9.2%, contracting 50 bps YoY due to Medi-Cal-like rate pressures in MassHealth and elevated malpractice costs, up 12% amid litigation trends. We're addressing this with $50 million in allocated capex for telehealth expansions and payer negotiations targeting 3% commercial rate uplifts in 2025.

Strategically, these margins underscore our focus on value-based care and operational resilience. We've embedded AI analytics from our Cerner bridge to Epic for real-time CMI forecasting, projecting another 1.5% CMI lift in Q3. Partnerships with payers like UnitedHealthcare and Blue Cross Blue Shield are accelerating bundled payments for MS-DRGs 470/471 (majors), now 22% of ortho volume, with shared savings exceeding $15 million YTD. Amid broader industry headwinds—rising drug prices from the IRA and ongoing cybersecurity risks post-Change Healthcare—we're prioritizing supply chain diversification, reducing single-vendor exposure by 25% on J&J and Medtronic products.

Looking ahead, we expect Q3 operating margins of 12.7% to 13.2%, with full-year FY24 at 12.8%, up 210 bps from FY23. This positions us for sustained 13%+ margins in FY25 as leverage compounds from our 5% admissions growth target and $200 million in enterprise-wide efficiencies.

Next, let's look at same-facility admissions and patient days, which continue to underscore the resilience and strategic positioning of our 45-hospital portfolio across 12 states. These metrics exclude the impact of our recent acquisitions, such as the three-hospital tuck-in in the Southeast earlier this year, allowing us to isolate organic performance at our mature facilities.

Starting with the headline numbers: On a same-facility basis, admissions grew 5.2% year-over-year, or YoY, in Q2, accelerating from 4.1% in Q1 and marking our strongest quarterly growth since Q4 2021. Quarter-over-quarter, or QoQ, admissions increased 1.1%, building on the seasonal tailwinds from summer elective volumes. Patient days followed suit, up 4.8% YoY and 0.9% QoQ, reflecting not just higher volumes but also modest pressure on average length of stay, or ALOS, which ticked up to 4.7 days from 4.6 days a year ago. This translated to an average daily census, or ADC, of 12,450 beds, a 4.9% YoY increase, with overall occupancy stabilizing at 68%, up from 65% in Q2 2023 but still below our pre-pandemic peak of 72%.

Let me drill down into the drivers. Admissions growth was broad-based across service lines, led by a robust 8.7% YoY increase in surgical admissions, fueled by the continued rebound in high-acuity electives like total joint replacements and spinal fusions. Our orthopedic volumes, in particular, surged 12% YoY, benefiting from pent-up demand and our expanded partnerships with leading ortho groups using robotic-assisted systems like the Mako platform from Stryker. Cardiovascular admissions grew 6.2% YoY, supported by our structural heart program expansions, including TAVR and MitraClip procedures, which saw a 15% uptick as we ramped transcatheter volumes in line with CMS coverage expansions.

On patient days, the 4.8% YoY growth was slightly tempered by a 0.4-day contraction in ALOS for non-surgical cases, driven by payer-mandated shorter stays under Medicare Advantage plans, which now represent 32% of our mix—up from 28% YoY. However, our case mix index, or CMI, rose 2.1% to 1.85, reflecting a shift toward higher-weighted DRGs in neuro and oncology. Oncology patient days jumped 9% YoY, aided by our infusion center optimizations and the rollout of CAR-T therapies in seven facilities.

Regionally, performance varied as expected. Our Sunbelt markets—Florida, Texas, and Arizona, which account for 55% of our bed capacity—delivered outsized growth, with same-facility admissions up 7.1% YoY and patient days +6.4%. Florida alone contributed 2,100 incremental admissions, propelled by strong snowbird seasonal inflows and our new freestanding ER feeder network, which boosted capture rates by 18%. In contrast, our Midwest and Northeast clusters faced headwinds from nursing shortages and flu/RSV seasonality, posting 2.8% YoY admissions growth and flat patient days QoQ. We've mitigated this through aggressive travel nurse reductions—down 45% from peak—and our proprietary workforce platform, UnityStaff, which filled 92% of shifts internally in Q2.

From a technical standpoint, our system-wide Epic MyChart implementation, now live in 85% of facilities, has been a game-changer for volume growth. Patient portal engagement hit 68% of discharges, driving a 22% increase in direct admissions via virtual triage tools, reducing ED boarding by 15%. We're also leveraging AI-driven predictive analytics from our partnership with Oracle Health to optimize bed turnover, which improved door-to-OR times by 12% and supported a 3% uptick in same-day surgery conversions without cannibalizing inpatient days.

Strategically, these trends affirm our focus on high-margin, high-acuity care amid the broader industry shift to outpatient and site-neutral payments. We're prudently expanding capacity with 250 brownfield ICU beds online by year-end, targeting a CMI lift to 1.90. Payer negotiations have locked in favorable rates—our commercial managed care index up 4.5%—while value-based contracts with UnitedHealthcare and Blue Cross plans now cover 25% of admissions, emphasizing quality metrics like readmissions, where we're at 14.2% versus the 15.8% peer average per HCUP data.

Looking ahead, we expect Q3 same-facility admissions growth of 4.5-5.5% YoY, with patient days at 4-5%, assuming normalized respiratory illness trends akin to 2019 baselines. Risks include potential Medicaid redeterminations post-unwinding, which could pressure 10% of our mix, but our diversified payer base and acuity focus position us well against peers like HCA and Tenet, who reported similar but slightly softer metrics last quarter.

Turning now to our capital expenditures, or CapEx, for facility modernization and expansion—a critical pillar of our long-term growth strategy at Unity Health Partners. In the first half of 2024, we deployed a total of $452 million in CapEx, representing a 16% increase from the $390 million invested in the first half of 2023. This acceleration reflects our disciplined approach to balancing near-term operational enhancements with multi-year capacity builds, all while targeting a blended return on invested capital, or ROIC, of 12-14% over the next five years.

Let me break this down for you. Approximately 62% of our first-half 2024 CapEx, or $280 million, went toward facility modernization initiatives across our 45-hospital footprint. The remainder—$172 million, or 38%—fueled expansion projects. For context, this is in line with industry peers like HCA Healthcare, which allocated about 55-60% to modernization in their recent quarters, and Universal Health Services, emphasizing similar tech-driven upgrades amid rising case mix index, or CMI, pressures.

Our modernization spend was heavily weighted toward technology integration and infrastructure refresh to support value-based care transitions and post-pandemic throughput recovery. Key highlights include:

EHR and Digital Infrastructure: We completed Phase 2 of our Epic MyChart rollout across 28 facilities, investing $85 million. This has already boosted patient portal adoption to 68%—up from 42% last year—and reduced length of stay by 0.4 days on average, directly contributing to a 2.2% lift in our adjusted admissions growth. We're on track to achieve full interoperability with payers like UnitedHealthcare and Humana by Q4 2024, positioning us for enhanced Medicare Advantage revenue, which now comprises 32% of our payer mix.

Imaging and OR Suite Upgrades: $72 million was allocated to next-gen diagnostic and procedural tech. This includes installing 12 new 3T MRI systems and eight 128-slice CT scanners from GE Healthcare and Siemens Healthineers, replacing equipment averaging 12 years old. In our high-acuity markets like the Southeast, these upgrades have improved scan volumes by 18% quarter-over-quarter, with early data showing a 15% reduction in no-show rates due to faster appointment turnaround.

Surgical Robotics and Hybrid ORs: We deployed five additional da Vinci Xi systems from Intuitive Surgical, at a cost of $28 million, focusing on our top 15 high-volume hospitals. This aligns with the industry's shift toward minimally invasive procedures, where robotics now account for 22% of our surgical case mix—mirroring Tenet Healthcare's playbook. We've also retrofitted 10 operating rooms into hybrid cath labs, enhancing our structural heart program and supporting a 9% YoY increase in cardiology DRG revenue.

Regionally, modernization has been prioritized in our legacy Midwest and Northeast markets, where facilities average 20+ years old. For instance, in the Rust Belt—think Cleveland and Pittsburgh metros—we've addressed deferred maintenance from the COVID drawdown, reducing our facilities' average age by 18 months system-wide. This has stabilized our inpatient days at 1.2 million annually while improving EBITDA margins by 120 basis points in those regions.

On the expansion side, our $172 million investment is laser-focused on high-growth ambulatory and inpatient capacity in the Sunbelt, where population inflows are driving 4-6% annual demand growth per CMS projections. Notable projects include:

Ambulatory Surgery Centers (ASCs) and Outpatient Pavilions: $95 million for three new greenfield ASCs in Texas (Dallas-Fort Worth) and Florida (Tampa Bay), plus expansions at two existing sites. These 12-OR facilities target high-margin ortho, GI, and pain management cases, with projected EBITDA margins of 35-40%—well above our inpatient average of 22%. We're modeling a 25% utilization ramp-up within 18 months, informed by peers like Surgery Partners, who've seen similar returns.

Inpatient Bed Adds and Specialty Wings: $52 million for 120 net new licensed beds, including a 48-bed behavioral health tower in Arizona's Phoenix MSA and ED expansions in Atlanta. This responds to the national shortage of psych beds—down 10% since 2010 per SAMHSA data—and our own 15% rise in ED volumes from migrant and retiree influxes.

Sustainability and Resilience Features: All expansions incorporate LEED Silver certifications and microgrid backups, costing an incremental 8% but yielding 20-year energy savings and qualifying for green bonds. In hurricane-prone Florida, we've elevated critical infrastructure per HCA's playbook post-Irma.

Strategically, these CapEx dollars are not just about bricks and mortar—they're about future-proofing against payer shifts and labor dynamics. With Medicare fee-for-service reimbursements flatlining at +2.5% for FY2025, our expansions emphasize outpatient migration, where we capture 85% of commercial rates. We're also partnering with Amazon Web Services for edge computing in telehealth-enabled wings, aiming to serve rural catchment areas underserved by competitors like Community Health Systems.

Looking ahead, we expect fiscal 2024 CapEx of $950 million, with modernization steady at ~60% and expansions ramping 12% to capture Sunbelt tailwinds. Payback periods average 4.5 years for modernization projects and 5-6 years for expansions, supported by 3-4% pricing leverage and volume growth from an aging boomer cohort—65+ admissions up 7% system-wide.

Finally, on our payer mix, which remains a cornerstone of our revenue stability and margin profile here at Unity Health Partners. Our diversified portfolio across 45 hospitals and 120 ambulatory surgery centers in the Southeast and Midwest continues to deliver predictable cash flows, even amidst the ongoing reimbursement headwinds from CMS and rising medical loss ratios among commercial payers.

For Q2, our net revenue payer mix shook out as follows: Medicare accounted for 46.2% of total net revenue, up 120 basis points year-over-year; Medicaid came in at 17.8%, flat sequentially but up modestly from 17.1% a year ago; commercial insurance, including managed care and fee-for-service, represented 29.4%, down 90 basis points YoY; and self-pay plus other sources made up the remaining 6.6%, which includes charity care write-offs and out-of-network balances post-No Surprises Act implementation.

Let me unpack the drivers here. Starting with Medicare, which continues to be our largest and most reliable payer, the uptick reflects the ongoing demographic tailwind from an aging population in our core markets. Our inpatient Medicare utilization grew 4.2% YoY, fueled by higher acuity cases—our case mix index, or CMI, rose to 1.68 from 1.62 last year—driven by procedures like hip and knee replacements and cardiac interventions. That said, we're feeling the pinch from the FY2025 IPPS final rule, where CMS cut the standardized amount by 2.9% after rebase and the productivity adjustment, partially offset by our strong documentation and HCC capture in the outpatient department, or OPD side. Medicare Advantage penetration in our markets now sits at 42%, up from 38% last year, and while star ratings have helped us secure bonus payments averaging $150 per member per month in our ACO REACH program—mirroring successes we've seen at peers like HCA Healthcare—prior authorization denials are up 15%, prompting us to invest $12 million this year in AI-driven denial management tools from Change Healthcare.

Medicaid held steady at 17.8%, benefiting from full expansion in our Florida, Georgia, and North Carolina footprints, where we've seen managed Medicaid rates stabilize post-redeterminations. Enrollment redeterminations earlier this year led to a 3% dip in our Medicaid member months in non-expansion states like Texas and Tennessee, but our supplemental payment programs—averaging $450 million annually system-wide—have cushioned the blow. We've outperformed the industry average here, with Medicaid days as a percentage of total inpatient days at 18.5% versus the 20% benchmark from the AHA's latest hospital statistics.

On the commercial side, the 29.4% mix reflects softer reimbursements amid MLR pressures at payers like UnitedHealthcare and Anthem Blue Cross Blue Shield. Our ASP-to-charge ratio for commercial payers dipped to 42% from 44% YoY, largely due to site-neutral payment policies eroding OPD margins on imaging and infusion services. Regionally, this was more acute in our Midwest cluster—think Indianapolis and Louisville—where commercial penetration is higher at 35% but contract renewals yielded only 2.5% rate increases versus our targeted 4%. Positively, our episodic payment bundles with Cigna for ortho and oncology have driven a 6% shift in high-margin commercial volume.

Self-pay and other ticked up slightly to 6.6%, but we've made strides in collections, boosting our self-pay AR yield to 28% from 24% through enhanced front-end eligibility screening via our Epic MyChart integration and partnerships with collectors like Ensemble Health. Charity care provisions rose to $85 million in Q2, aligned with our commitment under the 340B expansion, but bad debt expense as a percentage of revenue improved to 2.1% thanks to the No Surprises Act's arbitration wins—we resolved 65% of disputes in our favor at an average payment of 85% of billed charges.

Strategically, we're laser-focused on optimizing this mix for margin expansion. We've renegotiated 75% of our commercial contracts YTD, securing $220 million in incremental revenue over three years, with a push into value-based arrangements—now 22% of commercial revenue, up from 15%—including downside risk sharing in our CJR bundles for joints, similar to what Tenet Healthcare has scaled. Technologically, our $50 million investment in Cerner-to-Epic migration is paying off with 12% better HCC coding accuracy, directly lifting risk-adjusted reimbursements. Regionally, we're doubling down on Sunbelt growth: Florida's Medicare Advantage density gives us a 5% reimbursement edge over national averages, while our de novo ASCs in Georgia target commercial self-pay for cash procedures like cataracts, aiming to grow that segment to 8% of revenue by 2026.

Looking forward, we expect payer mix stability in Q3, with Medicare ticking up to 47% on seasonal flu and elective volume, commercial holding mid-20s% as we lap tougher comps, and self-pay trending down to 6% with continued eligibility tech. This positions us well for 3-4% net revenue growth in FY25, even if CMS's proposed 2.7% outpatient cut materializes.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Dr. Vasquez for an update on our clinical initiatives.

Dr. Elena Vasquez:
Thank you, Michael. Good morning. We are making significant progress in improving clinical outcomes and patient satisfaction. Our AI-powered predictive analytics program has shown promising results, with a 15% reduction in length-of-stay and a 12% drop in readmission rates. We are also focused on leveraging technology to enhance the patient experience and improve care coordination, including real-time bed management and sepsis detection tools that have exceeded CMS benchmarks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call back to Sarah.

Sarah Thompson:
Thank you, Dr. Vasquez. At this time, we will open the call for questions.

Operator:
Thank you. Our first question comes from Emily Carter with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Emily Carter:
Good morning. Can you provide more detail on the impact of the robotic-assisted surgery systems on your revenue growth and the impact on hospital efficiency?

Sarah Thompson:
Good morning, Emily. Thanks for the question. The rollout of da Vinci Xi systems and Mako platforms has been transformative. In Q2, these technologies drove a 20% uplift in high-acuity surgical volumes across our deployed sites, contributing roughly 1.5 percentage points to our overall revenue growth through higher CMI—up to 1.92—and 2.5x reimbursement premiums on inpatient procedures. Efficiency-wise, we've seen OR turnover times drop by 18%, enabling 12% more cases per suite daily, and a 15% reduction in LOS for ortho cases. This not only boosts throughput but also supports our value-based contracts by lowering readmissions. We're on track to deploy in 10 more hospitals by year-end, which should add another $100 million in annualized revenue while expanding EBITDA margins by 50 basis points. Robert can add more on ops if needed.

Operator:
Our next question comes from David Patel with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

David Patel:
What are your plans for expanding your network of hospitals and clinics in the coming year?

Robert Hayes:
Thanks, David. Our expansion strategy balances M&A tuck-ins with de novo builds to capture high-growth markets. We've already closed the $450 million acquisition adding 350 beds in Atlanta and Nashville, improving our commercial mix. Looking ahead 12 months, we're targeting 5-7% organic growth via 3-5 micro-hospitals in Florida and Texas suburbs—8-16 bed facilities focused on cardiology and orthopedics, leveraging freestanding ER feeders for 18% higher capture rates. Additionally, $172 million in CapEx this half funds three new ASCs and 120 inpatient beds, prioritizing Sunbelt demographics with 4-6% demand growth. This positions our 45-hospital footprint for resilient volumes amid redeterminations, with ROIC above 12%. We're also exploring two more tuck-ins in Midwest MSAs for scale.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Lisa Nguyen with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Lisa Nguyen:
Can you elaborate on the specific technologies you are implementing to improve care coordination?

Dr. Elena Vasquez:
Absolutely, Lisa. Care coordination is central to our model. Our Epic MyChart 2024 integration, live in 85% of facilities, drives 68% patient portal engagement, enabling virtual triage for 22% more direct admissions and 15% less ED boarding. Partnering with Google Cloud and Oracle Health, our AI predictive analytics handles real-time bed management, sepsis detection, and CMI forecasting, cutting LOS by 15% and readmissions by 12%—beating CMS HRRP benchmarks. Population health tools with Optum stratify 2.5 million lives, reducing total cost of care 18% for diabetics. Upcoming, edge computing with AWS for telehealth will extend rural reach. These have lifted patient satisfaction to the 75th percentile while supporting ACO savings of $45 million this quarter.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Mark Reynolds with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Mark Reynolds:
Thanks. On payer mix, with Medicare at 46%, how are you mitigating prior auth risks from MA plans?

Michael Chen:
Good question, Mark. Medicare Advantage at 42% penetration brings star rating bonuses—$150 PMPM in ACO REACH—but denials are up 15%, so we've invested $12 million in AI denial tools from Change Healthcare, improving overturn rates. HCC coding accuracy is up 12% post-Cerner-to-Epic, lifting risk-adjusted payments. Narrow-network contracts launching Q3 target 2-3% ASP uplift, and 22% of commercial is now value-based with downside protection. Regional edges like Florida's MA density give us a 5% reimbursement premium. Overall, this supports stable mix and 3-4% FY25 growth.

Sarah Thompson:
Thank you for the questions. In closing, I want to thank our dedicated employees for their hard work and commitment to providing high-quality care to our patients. We remain focused on executing our strategic priorities and delivering long-term value to our shareholders.

Jordan Lee:
Thank you for your participation in today's call. This concludes the Unity Health Partners Q2 2024 Earnings Conference Call. You may now disconnect.
